This paper proposes an AI-native industrial control paradigm, which reconceptualizes industrial control systems by positioning AI as the intrinsic core rather than an external enhancement. The proposed paradigm is built upon an AI-native infrastructure and a collection of collaborative agentic AIs, each encapsulating a set of advanced skills. Among them, the industrial control agent plays a central role in orchestrating the system lifecycle. Through this paradigm, industrial control shifts from a closed, capability-oriented, human-driven, and passive engineering process to an open, task-oriented, intent-driven, and autonomous solution delivery mechanism. The paper further analyzes the key challenges of the AI-native paradigm from both AI and industrial control perspectives, including issues related to AI model reliability, formal verification, real-time assurance, and heterogeneous resource orchestration. Overall, this work outlines a forward-looking vision for industrial control in the AI era and identifies critical research directions toward autonomous, evolvable, and adaptive control systems in complex and dynamic industrial environments.
item.dc:creator: Lisi Liu, Bin Wang, Quan Tang, Chuan Pang, Feng Gao, Shengkai Liu

item.title: Physical Adjoint Learning in Wave Systems with Asymmetric Couplings
item.description: arXiv:2610.34815v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Developing self-optimizing physical systems that learn directly from their response to external stimuli offers a promising route toward adaptive and intelligent machines. A key ingredient is the ability to evaluate optimization gradients within the physical hardware, bypassing the need for accurate numerical models. In wave systems, \textit{in-situ} adjoint methods provide this capability by exploiting reciprocity to physically realize the adjoint dynamics. However, this approach generally breaks down in nonreciprocal systems, where the adjoint field cannot be directly accessed through the original device. Here, we develop an \textit{in-situ} adjoint optimization framework that extends physical gradient computation to wave systems with asymmetric couplings through computationally low-cost similarity transformations between the forward and transposed operators. We utilize available degrees of freedom like tailored injected excitations, targeted measurements, and tunable parameters, to enable adjoint field reconstruction through forward experiments on the same physical platform. We demonstrate the versatility of the protocol through broadband transmission and isolation, coherent perfect absorption, programmable wavefront shaping, and spatially selective sensing. Our results provide a route to self-optimization in complex nonreciprocal wave systems through efficient physical gradient-based learning. The number of experiments required by the protocol does not increase with the number of optimization parameters, and the method remains applicable even when parts of the system are completely inaccessible.
item.dc:creator: Lucas J. Fern\'andez-Alc\'azar, John Guillamon, Krishna Joshi, Tsampikos Kottos

item.title: Physics-Informed and Data-Driven Composite Disturbance Separation and Predictive Control for Airborne Electro-Optical Gimbals with Multiple Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.34849v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper studies the constrained pointing control problem of airborne electro-optical gimbals subjected to composite periodic and aperiodic disturbances. Under carrier vibration, input delay, and actuator constraints, achieving line-of-sight stabilization and tracking is challenging. A disturbance-separated model predictive control (MPC) scheme is proposed to compensate these heterogeneous disturbances according to their physical characteristics. An adaptive periodic observer predicts multi-harmonic vibrations over the MPC horizon using linear-regression frequency estimation. A linear observer estimates the aperiodic disturbance, and a bounded long short-term memory (LSTM) network predicts its change over the input delay. Embedding periodic predictions into the MPC model while applying aperiodic compensation outside the optimizer limits amplification of aperiodic estimation errors and improves pointing accuracy under frequency changes and parameter mismatch. On the stated headroom envelope, input-set tightening provides feasible commands within the prescribed limits, and a regional practical tracking bound is established under explicit input-sequence and predicted-state margin conditions. A UAV-mounted two-axis gimbal platform is assembled for comparative indoor hovering experiments, complemented by simulations under frequency changes and parameter mismatch. In the reported trials, the proposed method achieves yaw and pitch relative-angle root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 0.770 degrees and 0.350 degrees, reducing tracking errors by 25.1% and 45.9% compared with linear active disturbance rejection control.
item.dc:creator: Yaokun Lu, Yifan Li, Zhixuan Zhang, Enmei Wang, Hao Teng, Jianzhong Qiao

item.title: Quantile-Based Command-Reserve MPC for Current-Command Gimbal Pointing
item.description: arXiv:2610.34913v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper studies the constrained line-of-sight pointing control problem of a two-axis current-command gimbal subjected to mismatched mechanical disturbances. Friction, torque ripple, current-response lag, model mismatch, and limited drive commands make accurate pointing more challenging yet interesting. A quantile disturbance predictor is proposed to compensate predictable acceleration residuals and describe their remaining uncertainty, with the aid of learning median and outer quantiles from state, command, and reference histories. A tube-inspired model predictive controller is proposed to reserve command headroom according to prediction uncertainty, with the aid of calibrated radii and stage-dependent input margins. The median improves the nominal prediction, while the radius adapts the command reserve without adding optimization variables. A finite-horizon tube inclusion result is established for a specified linear error model and fixed ancillary policy; its conditions are distinguished from the approximations used in hardware. Native command bounds and a final command limiter keep the sent commands within their prescribed range. On a two-axis embedded platform, four controller configurations are compared in seven repeated trials each. The proposed configuration achieves a two-dimensional pointing root-mean-square error of $3.94 \pm 0.10$ mrad with no command-limit samples in the evaluation windows. Its performance supports the combined use of residual prediction and adaptive command margins in the tested operating condition. Solver times and logged loop overruns are reported separately for the nominal 100 Hz implementation.
item.dc:creator: Yaokun Lu, Yifan Li, Enmei Wang, Hao Teng, Pengwei Hu, Jianzhong Qiao

item.title: Explicit Globally Asymptotically Stable Attitude Control with Reaction Wheel Angular Momentum and Torque Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.34922v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present an explicit Lyapunov attitude controller for rigid spacecraft actuated by three orthogonally mounted reaction wheels, parameterized using Modified Rodrigues Parameters (MRPs), which enforces hard bounds on wheel angular momentum and applied torque at every instant without solving any online optimization. A barrier-inspired momentum feedback prevents wheel saturation; a continuous positive scalar uniformly scales the feedback whenever a torque limit would otherwise be breached, preserving Lyapunov convergence. For the regulation problem, global asymptotic stability (GAS) is established via LaSalle's invariance principle, and constraint satisfaction is proved analytically for arbitrary symmetric positive-definite inertia matrices. Replacing the barrier by an error-state counterpart extends the design to tracking, with asymptotic (though no longer global) stability and the same safety guarantees under explicit feasibility conditions on the reference. Simulations confirm convergence and constraint satisfaction, and compare performance against other controllers.
item.dc:creator: Javier Urrios, Rafael Vazquez, Guillermo Pacheco-Ramos

item.title: Context-dependent Runtime Construction of Safe Regions of Attraction from Design-Time Identification for Multi-Candidate Simplex Architectures
item.description: arXiv:2610.35040v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deploying safety-critical cyber-physical systems requires control strategies that reconcile high performance and adaptability with rigorous safety guarantees. Classical control strategies offer stability proofs but are conservative, while advanced optimization- and learning-based controllers achieve high performance but lack formal verification. Runtime Assurance (RTA) architectures bridge this gap by introducing their own (dis-)advantages. Safety filters use online optimization and introduce chattering, while Simplex permissiveness is bounded by the tightness of the certified Region of Attraction (RoA) of its High-Assurance (HA) controller. Targeting this conservatism, we present a two-stage RoA certification procedure leveraging contraction-based stability to establish a target set for Taylor-model-based reachability analysis. We then treat the closed-loop system under HA control as a switched system, enabling: (a) runtime construction of context-dependent safe RoA and (b) safe switching between HA candidates to optimize recovery and maximize the operating envelope of the uncertified High-Performance (HP) controller. We validate this framework on a robotic path-tracking task using a three-stage evaluation: Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) simulation for theoretical verification, high-fidelity Gazebo simulation under unmodeled dynamics, and experiments on physical hardware. Results show that the Simplex architecture maintains safety under fault injection and successfully shields a behavioral-cloning-trained HP controller. Crucially, the decision module introduces negligible overhead (0.028 ms average, 4.13 ms worst-case), consuming under 10 % of the control period.
item.dc:creator: Georg J\"ager, Nils-Jonathan Friedrich, Norman Seyffer, Jos\'e Cec\'ilio, Ant\'onio Casimiro

item.title: A PDE-Based Model of Runner Flow in Mass Participation Events
item.description: arXiv:2610.35206v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents a macroscopic approach for modeling pedestrian movement. A convection-diffusion partial differential equation (PDE) is described and used to model the flow of runners along a marathon course. A marathon is a good modeling case study for human movement because the location of runners is only known in sparse locations, so an accurate model is needed to know where people are at all times. As well, marathons offer many safety and logistical problems that can be solved by modeling human movement. Data is obtained from the 2023 Columbus Marathon, and model improvements are made to include a temporally varying convection term. Results show an increase in model accuracy which can allow for better resource allocation and safety measures.
item.dc:creator: Alice Molinari, Brian Block, Stephanie Stockar, Simona Sacone

item.title: Trim: Fee Level Matters More Than Skew in Lightning Routing
item.description: arXiv:2610.35296v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Lightning routing nodes lend their channel balance for a posted fee. Operators' tools move that fee with the balance around a hand-set level, and which part of the fee drives revenue is unclear. We present Trim, which models a channel as a two-sided inventory with costly refills. Its optimal fee is a level, set by demand and replenishment, plus a balance skew, the shadow price of liquidity. The level is first order: no fee rule beats the ceiling demand and replenishment set, and on exactly solved channels the best flat fee comes within $1.6\%$ of the optimum at the median, whereas a level off by a factor of two loses tens of percent. The skew is second-order insurance: it adds at most what the flow-balancing flat fee loses to refused forwards. So the level should be chosen: Trim's rule traces the revenue--success frontier, posts one level on every channel, and adds a skew only where refills stay frequent and costly. On a 2026 snapshot with synthetic payments, no tuned tool beats that frontier by over a few percent, and a skew changes gross revenue by a few percent.
item.dc:creator: Huiping Sun, Peilu Guo, Yiming Zhu, Yueqi Wu, Zhong Chen

item.title: ADACT: PDE-Constrained Thermal Hardware/Software Co-Design Adjoint-Driven Optimal Control via Finite Difference Discretization
item.description: arXiv:2610.35569v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: By virtue of the sheer compute demands of large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC), modern multi-core microprocessors suffer from severe power density limits and thermal throttling, entailing an urgent need for principled methods for predictive, physics-informed dynamical thermal management (DTM). Here, we introduce a hardware/software co-design physics-informed PDE-constrained DTM throttling optimal control algorithm, ADACT (Adjoint-Driven Adaptive Co-Design Thermal Control), that minimizes thermal risk and cooling energy overhead while maximizing core execution throughput. The underlying physical temperature field is governed by a two-dimensional nonhomogeneous parabolic reaction-diffusion equation with spatially localized, time-varying power source terms and variable convective cooling subject to nonhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. We employ a discretization of the continuous state PDE via a Crank-Nicolson finite difference scheme with a 5-point discrete Laplacian operator on a uniform spatial mesh, which preserves unconditional numerical stability and $O(\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta t^2)$ second-order temporal and spatial accuracy. To efficiently compute exact gradients, we construct and implement a continuous backward-in-time adjoint state method with L-BFGS as our optimization algorithm of choice. The accuracy and second-order convergence rates of both forward state and backward adjoint solvers are quantitatively verified via the Method of Manufactured Solutions (MMS), and gradient accuracy is validated using directional derivative Taylor tests. Numerical experiments demonstrate that ADACT dynamically throttles software power workloads and modulates hardware cooling efforts to strictly uphold physical thermal thresholds while maintaining operational throughput.
item.dc:creator: Don Li

item.title: Efficient ADMM for Soft-Constrained Quadratic Programs via Generalized Slack Projections
item.description: arXiv:2610.35631v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quadratic programs (QPs) are a core building block in many applications. In practice, constraints are often softened with slack variables to guarantee feasibility. The standard approach tackles this by introducing additional decision variables, growing the resulting optimization problem. In this paper, we propose an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) scheme for a broad class of convex slack penalty functions, including all $\ell_k$-norms, without increasing the problem size. The only change to the ADMM scheme is a modified slack projection function, while the remaining algorithm stays the same. We demonstrate our approach on numerical examples, showing significant speedups, and show its flexibility on an energy optimization problem.
item.dc:creator: Roland Schwan, Thomas Lew, Brian Plancher

item.title: World Model for Energy Efficiency Maximization in Dynamic Metasurface Antennas
item.description: arXiv:2610.35813v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dynamic metasurface antennas (DMAs) have emerged as a promising technology for realizing large-scale antenna arrays in next-generation wireless networks owing to their ability to enable dense and energy-efficient antenna architectures. However, jointly optimizing digital beamforming and DMA element weights under time-varying channel conditions remains challenging due to their coupled effects on the received signal and interference powers. We formulate this problem to maximize time-averaged energy efficiency (EE) under time-varying channel conditions, subject to transmit power constraints, Lorentzian phase limitations, and minimum rate requirements. To enable long-term planning and improve sample efficiency compared with model-free reinforcement learning, we develop a world model framework that learns latent system dynamics from interactions with the environment and jointly optimizes digital beamforming and DMA element weights through imagined trajectories. Furthermore, we incorporate feasibility-preserving action mappings and safety cost signals to ensure constraint satisfaction during policy learning. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves the time-averaged EE by approximately 20% compared with the deep Q-network baseline, while achieving higher sample efficiency and more reliable constraint satisfaction.
item.dc:creator: Abdolrasoul Sakhaei Gharagezlou, Mehdi Monemi, Matti Latva-aho, Mehdi Rasti

item.title: Learning Force-Reactive Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35862v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many everyday tasks require controlling contact force as well as motion. On a humanoid, this force must often be coordinated across both hands and the whole body, and cannot be specified by kinematic trajectories alone. Therefore, we present FLORE, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. We collect robot-free demonstrations using two force-sensing UMI-style handheld grippers for hand motion and contact wrenches, and wearable trackers for body motion. A force-reactive diffusion policy takes vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches as input, then predicts actions and per-hand force commands. A hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking executes these commands while maintaining balance: an integral of the force error measured by real force/torque (F/T) sensors lets each hand track force accurately along the commanded direction and remain compliant along the others. In simulation, the controller tracks per-hand force commands of varied magnitude and direction, with little loss in whole-body motion accuracy. Across three contact-rich tasks on the robot, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller. For more details, please visit our website: https://louis-leee.github.io/FLoRe/.
item.dc:creator: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi

item.title: Windex: Index-Driven Contextual Scheduler for Scalable Service Guarantees in NextG Cellular Networks
item.description: arXiv:2406.01888v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Next-generation cellular networks must support heterogeneous service objectives, ranging from throughput-oriented eMBB to latency- and regularity-constrained URLLC and XR traffic. Enforcing these objectives at the RAN scheduler is difficult because wireless channels, queues, and application arrivals evolve at the millisecond timescale while spectrum resources are shared across users. We formulate service-aware RAN scheduling as a constrained Markov decision process with per-user throughput and service-regularity constraints. A Lagrangian relaxation gives an exact decomposition of the relaxed problem into per-user control problems with a common resource price. We prove fixed-dual indexability for an illustrative time-since-last-service (TSLS) debt arm with a throughput objective and TSLS constraint, note the analogous scalar throughput-debt result, and assume fixed-dual indexability for the full vector state used in deployment. We design Windex, an index-driven scheduler that learns dual-dependent per-user break-even resource prices using compact neural approximators over queue, channel, TSLS, and violation-deficit state. We further design CWindex, a contextual extension that infers service class from queue-history time series when explicit labels are unavailable. We implement Windex as an application compatible with a realtime 5G radio intelligent controller. Inference takes 10-20 $\mu$s per user on a general-purpose CPU, well within a 1 ms control budget. Trace-driven emulation using over-the-air channel measurements and larger simulations show that Windex and CWindex substantially reduce per-user service violations while maintaining throughput efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Archana Bura, Ushasi Ghosh, Alexander Riedel, Dinesh Bharadia, Srinivas Shakkottai

item.title: Minimum Time Consensus of Multi-agent System under Fuel Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2407.19927v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work addresses the problem of finding the minimum time consensus point in the state space for a set of $N$ identical double integrator agents with bounded input and fixed fuel budget constraints. The attainable set of each agent under these constraints is computed, and its boundary is used to characterize the set of initial conditions from which consensus is possible. The minimum time to consensus is the least time at which the attainable sets of all agents intersect, and the corresponding consensus state is their point of intersection. Using convexity of the attainable set and Helly's theorem, this reduces to examining the triplets of agents, for which a closed-form expression for the minimum time and the consensus point is obtained. The triplet computations are independent and are distributed evenly among the $N$ agents. The overall minimum time and consensus point are given by the triplet with the greatest minimum time, and each agent then computes its own control input locally. An example with $12$ agents is used to illustrate the results.
item.dc:creator: Akansha Rautela, Deepak Patil, Ameer Mulla, Indra Narayan Kar

item.title: Describing Functions and Phase Response Curves of Excitable Systems
item.description: arXiv:2511.16235v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The describing function (DF) and phase response curve (PRC) are classical tools for the analysis of feedback oscillations and rhythmic behaviors, widely used across control engineering, biology, and neuroscience. These tools are known to have limitations in networks of relaxation oscillators and excitable systems. For this reason, the paper proposes a novel approach tailored to excitable systems. Our analysis focuses on the discrete-event operator mapping input trains of events to output trains of events. The methodology is illustrated on the excitability model of Hodgkin-Huxley. The proposed framework provides a basis for designing and analyzing central pattern generators in networks of excitable neurons, with direct relevance to neuromorphic control and neurophysiology.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 2026 European Control Conference (ECC) (2026) 2369-2374
item.dc:creator: Robin Wroblowski, Rodolphe Sepulchre

item.title: Multi-Agentic AI for Fairness-Aware and Accelerated Multi-modal Large Model Inference in Real-world Mobile Edge Networks
item.description: arXiv:2602.07215v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has transformed applications in natural language processing and content creation, yet centralized inference remains hindered by high latency, limited customizability, and privacy concerns. Deploying large models (LMs) in mobile edge networks emerges as a promising solution. However, it also poses new challenges, including heterogeneous multi-modal LMs with diverse resource demands and inference speeds, varied prompt/output modalities that complicate orchestration, and resource-limited infrastructure ill-suited for concurrent LM execution. In response, we propose a Multi-Agentic AI framework for latency- and fairness-aware multi-modal LM inference in mobile edge networks. Our solution includes a long-term Global Planning Agent, a short-term Prompt Scheduling Agent, and multiple on-node LM Deployment Agents, all powered by foundation language models. These agents cooperatively optimize prompt routing and LM deployment through natural language reasoning over runtime telemetry and historical experience. To evaluate its performance, we further develop a city-wide testbed that supports network monitoring, containerized LM deployment, intra-server resource management, and inter-server communications. Experiments demonstrate that our solution reduces average end-to-end latency by 42.9% compared with a state-of-the-art online-learning baseline and by 80.6% compared with the full-activation baseline, while maintaining a mean service-type Jain's index of 0.925. Moreover, our solution adapts quickly without fine-tuning, offering a generalizable solution for optimizing GenAI services in edge environments.
item.dc:creator: Haiyuan Li, Hari Madhukumar, Shuangyi Yan, Yulei Wu, Dimitra Simeonidou

item.title: Stability and stabilization of semilinear single-track vehicle models with distributed tire friction dynamics via singular perturbation analysis
item.description: arXiv:2602.08757v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper investigates the stability and stabilization of semilinear single-track vehicle models with distributed tire friction dynamics, modeled as interconnections of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs). Motivated by the long-standing practice of neglecting transient tire dynamics in vehicle modeling and control, a rigorous justification is provided for such simplifications using singular perturbation theory. A perturbation parameter, defined as the ratio between a characteristic rolling contact length and the vehicle's longitudinal speed, is introduced to formalize the time-scale separation between rigid-body motion and tire dynamics. For sufficiently small values of this parameter, it is demonstrated that standard finite-dimensional techniques can be applied to analyze the local stability of equilibria and to design stabilizing controllers. Whilst the proposed controllers build on classical approaches, the novelty of this work lies in establishing the first singular perturbation framework for ODE-PDE vehicle models with distributed tire dynamics, providing a theoretical justification for their quasi-static reduction and for the use of finite-dimensional tools for analysis and control design.
item.dc:creator: Luigi Romano, Ole Morten Aamo, Miroslav Krsti\'c, Jan {\AA}slund, Erik Frisk

item.title: Data-based Low-conservative Nonlinear Safe Control Learning
item.description: arXiv:2604.01156v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a data-driven safe control framework for nonlinear discrete-time systems with parametric uncertainty and additive disturbances. The proposed approach constructs a data-consistent closed-loop representation that enables controller synthesis and safety certification directly from data. Unlike existing methods that treat unmodeled nonlinearities as global worst-case uncertainties using Lipschitz bounds, the proposed approach embeds nonlinear terms directly into the invariance conditions via a geometry-aware difference-of-convex formulation. This enables facet- and direction-specific convexification, avoiding both nonlinearity cancellation and the excessive conservatism induced by uniform global bounds. We further propose a vertex-dependent controller construction that enforces convexity and contractivity conditions locally on the active facets associated with each vertex, thereby enlarging the class of certifiable invariant sets. For systems subject to additive disturbances, disturbance effects are embedded directly into the verification conditions through optimized, geometry-dependent bounds, rather than via uniform margin inflation, yielding less conservative robust safety guarantees. As a result, the proposed methods can certify substantially larger safe sets, naturally accommodate joint state and input constraints, and provide data-driven safety guarantees. The simulation results show a significant improvement in both nonlinearity tolerance and the size of the certified safe set.
item.dc:creator: Amir Modares, Bahare Kiumarsi, Hamidreza Modares

item.title: Distributed Optimization with Nesterov Momentum and Finite-Time Quantized Averaging over Directed Networks: Extended Version
item.description: arXiv:2604.16906v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In modern large-scale networked systems, rapidly solving optimization problems while utilizing communication resources efficiently is critical for addressing complex tasks. However, distributed optimization over bandwidth-limited networks must cope with two obstacles: limited-bandwidth communication, and slow convergence when the objective is ill-conditioned. In this paper, we consider unconstrained distributed optimization over strongly connected directed networks, where nodes exchange quantized (i.e., compressed) messages. We propose QANM (Quantized Averaged Nesterov Momentum), an algorithm that combines Nesterov momentum with a finite-time quantized averaging protocol. At every iteration, QANM enables all nodes to reach exact agreement, without requiring doubly stochastic weight matrices or undirected communication. For strongly convex and smooth objectives, we show that the objective gap of QANM decays at the accelerated rate $1-\kappa^{-1/2}$ (where $\kappa$ is the condition number), up to a residual of order $\Delta^2$ determined by the quantization level $\Delta$. This improves the condition-number dependence of the transient iteration complexity from $\kappa$ to $\sqrt{\kappa}$ compared with gradient descent that utilizes the same quantized averaging mechanism. Finally, we evaluate QANM on a distributed sensor fusion problem, showing that our algorithm exhibits the fastest initial error reduction compared with other methods from current literature.
item.dc:creator: Ruochen Wu, Xu Du, Mohammadreza Doostmohammadian, Karl H. Johansson, Apostolos I. Rikos

item.title: Fair Dynamic Operating Envelopes using Distributed Multi-Period Optimal Power Flow and Jain Index for Active Distribution Networks
item.description: arXiv:2608.23444v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dynamic operating envelopes (DOEs) are increasingly used to publish time-varying export limits that keep distribution networks within operational limits. Purely technical DOE allocation, however, can systematically privilege electrically favorable prosumers, while embedding fairness directly into a single-period optimal power flow (OPF) objective mixes network feasibility, equity and efficiency in a way that obscures the cost of fairness. This paper proposes a two-stage, multi-period framework that addresses both of these. Initially, a technical distributed OPF computes network-feasible export envelopes. The subsequent stage then applies a dynamic aggregate export budget and redistributes capacity through cumulative proportional fairness, limiting the additional curtailment by an admissible efficiency budget. The resulting fair DOEs are treated as first-stage decisions, while battery storage provides scenario-dependent recourse under demand and renewable uncertainty. The operational problem is solved by a calibrated regional alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) on a lossless LinDistFlow model and independently validated using AC power flow. We observe a trade-off between increases in curtailment \emph{versus} improvements on fairness, as expected, reaching Jain fairness indices close to unity. Results show that considering both storage (which alleviates curtailment impact) and multi-period fairness (which increases curtailment) is an interesting approach for modern DOE design, which in turn requires a multi-period, co-designed approach.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Salom\~ao Quessongo, Daniel Gebbran, Clodomiro Unsihuay-Vila

item.title: Uncertainty-Aware Parameter Estimation for Condition Monitoring of Power Converters
item.description: arXiv:2609.00218v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Changes in circuit parameters can indicate component degradation in power converters, but measurement noise and limited parameter observability can make these changes difficult to detect reliably. This paper proposes an uncertainty-aware parameter estimation framework to distinguish genuine parameter changes from variations caused by estimation uncertainty. Using a differentiable switched converter model, the method requires only one or two samples per switching period. Model-derived residual whitening and a Bayesian posterior approximation quantify estimation uncertainty and reveal poorly identifiable parameters. Simulations demonstrate improved estimation accuracy over least-squares and physics-informed neural-network benchmarks, with uncertainty estimates consistent with repeated noise realizations. Experiments on a laboratory buck converter validate the estimated parameters against independently derived references and demonstrate the detection of a controlled output-capacitance reduction. The proposed framework provides a basis for reliable parameter-change detection in power converter condition monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Tomas Monopoli, Jiahong Liu, Shuai Zhao

item.title: Low-Altitude Platform Stations for Dense Urban Connectivity
item.description: arXiv:2609.10414v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper evaluates the downlink performance of 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) realized via low-altitude platform station (LAPS)-mounted base stations, and compares it against conventional 5G terrestrial network (TN) in a realistic dense urban scenario. Using a 3GPP-compliant multi-cell hexagonal layout with 19 sites and 57 sectors, we model LAPS altitudes ranging from 100 to 1000 m and evaluate the average effective signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio and user throughput via system-level simulations. Results show that LAPS-based NTN deployments can significantly outperform terrestrial 5G in per-user throughput, provided the LAPS altitude is properly chosen to balance increased line-of-sight probability against inter-beam interference.

item.title: Rethinking electrified transportation: The case for dynamic wireless charging
item.description: arXiv:2610.18708v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-term infrastructure investment often requires choosing between an established technology and a capital-intensive alternative that gains value as demand matures. For electric vehicle (EV) charging, this trade-off is between incumbent stationary charging technology and emerging dynamic wireless charging (DWC). DWC could fundamentally alter transportation electrification by enabling high-throughput charging in motion and reducing reliance on large onboard batteries; however, its high upfront cost makes the timing and location of deployment critical. Overcommitting to stationary charging stations (SCS) risks technological lock-in and forgoing the benefits of DWC, whereas premature DWC deployment can strand capital in underutilized corridors. Through a joint investment assessment framework coupling DWC, SCS, and supporting grid infrastructure across nearly 49,000 miles of the US Interstate freight network, we find that higher utilization and longer project lifetimes rapidly shift investment toward DWC, whose share rises sharply from 48% at a project lifetime of 30 years to 100% at 32 years. Contiguous DWC segments can share grid connections, enabling them to provide over six times the rated charging capacity of SCS while requiring 46% less investment in new distribution-grid infrastructure. We also find that a combined DWC and SCS portfolio reaches a maximum lifetime value of USD 60 billion, 63% above the case with only SCS. We further identify specific traffic demand, construction, and grid access conditions that shape where each technology becomes advantageous, yielding actionable thresholds for SCS and DWC deployment that directly inform long-term EV charging infrastructure investment and policy.

item.title: Convex Inner Approximations for Safe AC Dispatch With Device Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.26634v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Safe AC dispatch requires both feasible operating points and enough ramping capability to reach the next target. This paper constructs convex inner approximations that connect nonlinear network feasibility, constrained device response, and dispatch-interval tracking. A fixed-point certificate enforces AC operating limits under bounded load uncertainty. Componentwise response envelopes convert heterogeneous device dynamics into affine conditions on measured states and power references. A command governor then combines these conditions with available ramping capability and a hard terminal-error bound. It selects an admissible target through a minimum-deviation objective and holds the corresponding reference while reserved fast regulation remains active. The resulting quadratic program optimizes controllable references and auxiliary variables. Tests on the IEEE 39- and 118-bus systems include 96 single-target executions and 64 transitions in continuous dispatch sequences at five- and fifteen-minute intervals. All 160 transitions satisfy the AC constraints, independent balancing-generator capability checks, and the prescribed regulation-adjusted terminal accuracy. Complete admission-cycle medians are 3.45 and 8.79 ms. A connected synthetic system with 3,200 buses and 1,000 generating units extends the computational assessment to 999 independent references, with a median cycle time of \LargeMedian{} s. The construction provides a tractable link between available ramping capability and safe, timely execution of AC dispatch.

item.title: Why the Swing Parameters Are Sloppy
item.description: arXiv:2610.30084v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evangelou, Stankovi\'c, Kevrekidis and Transtrum compared analytic and data-driven assessments of parameter identifiability for the infinite-bus synchronous generator. Fisher information with the manifold boundary approximation method (MBAM), and output diffusion maps with geometric harmonics, report the same six identifiable parameters on the late window $t \in [3, 5]\text{ s}$, and both place the inertia $H$ and the damping $D$ among the unidentifiable ones. We explain this result from the geometry of the dynamics rather than from that of the parameter-to-data map. The rotor swing is a fast fibre that has collapsed onto a two-dimensional normally attracting invariant manifold (NAIM) of the transient fluxes before the window opens. The zeroth-order NAIM is exactly independent of $H$, $D$, $T_{d0}''$ and $T_{q0}''$, four of the five MBAM limits. We prove, under stated smoothness and rank conditions, that each of the four limits is a boundary of the model manifold at a distance equal, to first order in the parameter, to its current profiled speed. The same analysis predicts how identifiability changes with the experiment: neither a larger initial speed deviation nor a load change restores $H$ or $D$ in the late window, whereas the early window $[0, 2]\text{ s}$ makes $H$ the best-determined parameter. Evaluated in a physical metric fixed by synchrophasor accuracy limits, the late window identifies five parameters rather than six and the early window nine. The spiked-covariance structure of the linearised trajectory map explains why the principal components of whitened, sampled trajectories reproduce the prior-scaled Fisher spectrum, and regression on those components attains the Fisher-predicted recovery error in 113 of 114 parameter--scenario pairs.

item.title: Asymmetric-Information Resource Allocation Games: An LP Approach to Purposeful Deception
item.description: arXiv:2604.25070v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, we introduce the Deceptive Resource Allocation Game (DRAG), which studies purposeful deception within a Bayesian game framework. In DRAG, a Defender allocates resources across the true asset and several decoys to influence an Attacker's beliefs and actions, with the goal of diverting the Attacker away from the true asset. We seek to characterize purposeful deception, whereby the Defender deceives only when doing so improves its performance. To this end, we solve for the Perfect Bayesian Nash Equilibrium (PBNE) of the corresponding game. We show that, despite the coupled belief-policy interdependence, the problem admits an efficient, non-iterative linear programming formulation. Numerical results demonstrate that the resulting policies naturally balance effective allocation and belief manipulation, giving rise to purposeful and emergent deceptive behaviors.

item.title: PREFER: Personalized Review Summarization with Online Preference Learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.05911v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Product reviews significantly influence purchasing decisions on e-commerce platforms. However, the sheer volume of reviews can overwhelm users, obscuring information most relevant to their individual needs. Existing e-commerce summarization systems typically produce generic, static summaries that fail to account for the fact that (i) different users prioritize different product characteristics, and (ii) these preferences may evolve with interactions. To address these challenges, we propose an online learning framework that generates personalized summaries for each user by representing user interests in a latent aspect space and selecting preference-aligned review evidence. Our system then iteratively refines its understanding of user preferences by incorporating feedback on the generated summaries directly over time. We evaluate our framework on Amazon Reviews'23 using controlled feedback simulations and robustness checks with held-out-history, independent-embedding, and external LLM-based evaluators. These experiments show improvements in preference-aligned evidence selection under the evaluated feedback settings. A separate human-based study finds that scenario-conditioned summaries are preferred over generic (uniformly-aggregated) alternatives in 69.9% of paired comparisons.

item.title: SateBeam: Beam-Aware Radio Map Estimation With Physics-Consistent Parametric Modeling for Unknown Multiple Satellites
item.description: arXiv:2605.07763v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dense low-Earth-orbit (LEO) networks increasingly reuse spectrum across moving satellites and overlapping beams, making a spatial radio map essential for interference diagnosis and coordination. Constructing such a map from sparse ground power measurements is difficult because the active satellite subset and its cardinality are unknown, candidate footprints can be highly coherent, and beam pointing, width, effective power, Doppler, and background must be inferred jointly. Known ephemerides do more than enumerate visible candidates. Propagated positions determine candidate-specific ranges, viewing geometry, and spatial footprints, while radial velocities induce distinct time-frequency signatures. Their joint spatial--Doppler structure rejects candidates whose geometry or time--frequency signature conflicts with the observations before continuous beam inference. SateBeam therefore screens all candidates through Doppler-resolved nonnegative fitting. GPU-accelerated grid correlations initialize continuous off-grid refinement; a Gamma-likelihood Bayesian information criterion (BIC) selects model cardinality, and backward deletion and exchange repair greedy support errors. Across paired real-ephemeris scenarios, SateBeam recovers the exact support in every case and reduces independent-query RMSE from $0.655$ to $0.050$ dB relative to orthogonal matching pursuit, with consistent advantages under model mismatch and larger candidate sets. The code is available at https://github.com/UNIC-Lab/SateBeam.

item.title: Crazyflow: An Accurate, GPU-Accelerated, Differentiable Drone Simulator in JAX
item.description: arXiv:2606.01478v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-quality, large-scale synthetic data from simulations is becoming a cornerstone for pushing robots' capabilities. While aerial robotics simulators have evolved to support specialized needs such as fidelity, differentiability, and swarms independently, a unified platform that synthesizes data across all these domains is missing. In this work, we propose Crazyflow, a simulator designed to push the frontier of aerial robotics algorithm development, supporting model-based and data-driven methods, gradient-based and sampling-based approaches, single- and multi-agent systems, and state- and vision-based policy learning. Crazyflow combines high-fidelity dynamics with JAX for speed and differentiability, scaling to millions of environments or thousands of swarms with thousands of drones on single CPUs and GPUs, and beyond on clusters. Real-world experiments show Crazyflow supports both analytical-gradient-based policy learning, achieving high-accuracy tracking without domain randomization, and sampling-based obstacle avoidance at speeds exceeding half a billion steps per second. Breaking the traditional train-then-deploy paradigm, Crazyflow's performance enables in-flight reinforcement learning; we demonstrate this by throwing a physical drone into the air and training a recovery policy from scratch in 0.37 seconds, catching it before it hits the ground. By pushing accuracy, speed, and differentiability simultaneously, Crazyflow serves as an open-source resource for synthetic data generation, with emerging capabilities for large-scale parallelization for online, in-execution learning and optimization, opening the door to novel algorithm development.

item.title: Shooting for Contact: Contact-Implicit Multiple Shooting for Dynamic Motion Retargeting
item.description: arXiv:2608.03116v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Motion retargeting approaches often prioritize kinematic similarity over whole-body dynamics, contact consistency, and actuation limits, yielding references that are difficult for reinforcement learning (RL) policies to reproduce, particularly for contact-rich behaviors. We present a contact-implicit, direct simulation-based multiple shooting (DSMS) framework that transforms kinematically feasible references into dynamically feasible whole-body trajectories. By embedding a differentiable simulator within a nonlinear program, DSMS resolves contact, friction, impacts, self-collision, and joint limits internally while enforcing tracking, actuation, and task constraints without prescribing a contact schedule or introducing explicit contact constraints. Compared with existing retargeting methods, DSMS accelerates motion-imitation RL training and yields policies with high success rates and low tracking error. We further demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on the Unitree G1 through command-conditioned walking, jogging, and contact-rich crawling, and a highly dynamic 180-degree jump-turn.

item.title: GPU-Accelerated Quantum Annealing-Inspired UAV Path Planning for Smart Agriculture
item.description: arXiv:2608.25376v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: With the rapid advancement of smart agriculture, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have become indispensable for efficient coverage and path planning in grid-mapped agricultural fields. However, optimizing UAV flight paths in large-scale environments remains a complex Nondeterministic Polynomial-time (NP)-hard problem. Traditional path planning methods are often constrained by local optima, limited scalability, and slow convergence, which significantly restrict their effectiveness in solving large-scale problems. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel optimization framework utilizing a Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)-parallelized Ising solver. Our method mimics the operational principles of quantum annealing on GPU hardware, enabling rapid search for the minimum-energy state of Ising models. Unlike physical quantum devices, which are often constrained by the number of qubits, our approach leverages the Fixstars Amplify (FA) platform to perform parallel annealing on highly parallelized GPUs. This enables the simultaneous evaluation of thousands of potential path candidates and vast state transitions. By leveraging large-scale parallel processing, this framework's core strength lies in minimizing computation time even as the problem scale increases. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed method consistently identifies superior flight paths while maintaining stable computational performance compared with the genetic algorithm and simulated annealing method.

item.title: On the invariance of risk-sensitive LQR gain under input randomization
item.description: arXiv:2609.02363v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper shows that the optimal gain of the risk-sensitive linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problem is invariant under input randomization when the cost penalizes the realized noisy input. This may appear counterintuitive at first glance because certainty equivalence does not hold for risk-sensitive LQR and input randomization inflates the effective process noise. Nonetheless, the gain is preserved because the input noise enters not only the system dynamics but also the cost functional, and its total effect eventually vanishes. Consequently, the optimal gain and the Riccati recursion need not be recomputed, and the increment in the optimal cost can be readily evaluated in closed form. This result facilitates the use of risk-sensitive LQR in applications that employ input randomization for privacy or exploration, such as dynamic watermarking for replay attack detection.

item.title: VLN on the Fly: An Onboard Vision-Language Navigation Stack for Aerial Robots
item.description: arXiv:2609.20191v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Running vision-language navigation fully onboard an aerial robot is hard, since grounding, planning, and control must share limited compute and a single-stage error is difficult to isolate in flight. End-to-end aerial policies fuse these stages into one network, giving up the observability and safety checks a modular stack keeps available. We propose VLN on the Fly, an onboard stack that keeps grounding, planning, and control as separate, inspectable stages. A quantized VLM grounds an instruction to a coarse image cell, depth lifts it to a 3D goal, a fast B-spline planner returns a feasible trajectory, and a pretrained reinforcement learning policy tracks it to motor commands across quadrotors. Across 15 onboard flights over three everyday referents in a controlled indoor volume, the stack reaches the target in 13 of 15 trials with 5.72 cm mean goal error and 39.3% average GPU utilization. In 6 additional cluttered-environment trials, the stack tracks collision-free trajectories under onboard perception gating.

item.title: A Novel Path-Tracking Algorithm for Automated Tractor-Trailer Forward and Backward Maneuvers
item.description: arXiv:2609.21718v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fully autonomous tractor-trailer systems are increasingly deployed in logistics, agriculture, and industrial environments, where precise and robust path-tracking capabilities are essential. However, the articulation between the tractor and the trailer introduces additional nonlinearities and significantly complicates lateral and longitudinal control, particularly during reversing maneuvers. This paper introduces a novel path-tracking algorithm specifically designed for articulated vehicles with a single trailer. The proposed method combines a lateral control law applied at the trailer level with a short-horizon predictive adjustment of the tractor steering angle, ensuring stable convergence toward the desired path in both forward and backward motion. The approach is geometry-based and requires no per-vehicle calibration or training. Simulation studies in a high-fidelity physics simulator show steady-state or final lateral errors of $0.02$--$0.05$~m on straight-line, circular, and reverse docking trajectories, which is of the same order of magnitude as, or lower than, the errors reported in the literature. Real-world experiments on a small-scale tractor--trailer robot, with the whole controller running on a low-cost microcontroller, further confirm the feasibility of the approach, with lateral errors below 13~mm during repeated reverse docking maneuvers despite a pose detection latency of about 200~ms.
item.dc:creator: Alexandre Lombard, Florent Perronnet, Th\'eo Rigal, Nicolas Gaud, Abdeljalil Abbas-Turki

item.title: Symmetry-breaking in a discrete-choice LQG mean field game
item.description: arXiv:2610.05730v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mean-field games provide a continuum framework for modeling the dynamics of large, interacting populations of non-cooperative agents. This paper studies symmetry-breaking in a finite-horizon, two-choice min-LQG mean-field game in which identical agents with linear stochastic dynamics choose one of two equally desirable terminal destinations, while trading off control effort against social pressure to conform. The model has an odd symmetry between the two destinations and therefore always admits a symmetric, dynamic Nash equilibrium in which the population splits evenly between them, producing a deadlock collective state at final time. Numerical studies have suggested that, as the penalty for social nonconformity increases, this symmetric equilibrium loses stability as a fixed point of an associated scalar, self-consistency map, and asymmetric consensus Nash equilibria emerge, where most agents select the same destination. By analyzing the linearized forward-backward PDE system through the scalar map representation, we provide a proof of this loss of stability of the symmetric equilibrium. Together with the odd symmetry of the map, this implies the existence of symmetry-broken mean-field game equilibria corresponding to consensus on either destination.
